extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, legal researchers, practitioners, and others interested in U.S. federal rulemaking and the Federal Register
extracted.subtask_description: An informational overview of the U.S. Federal Register: what it contains, how it is organized and cited, how it interfaces with the notice-and-comment (NPRM) process, and where it can be accessed (including APIs and commercial services).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of the Federal Register
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Register is the official journal of the federal government that contains government agency rules, proposed rules, and public notices. It provides a means for the government to announce to the public changes to government requirements, policies, and guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific types of content include proposed new rules, final rules, changes to existing rules, notices of meetings and adjudicatory proceedings, and presidential documents (executive orders, proclamations, administrative orders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) / notice-and-comment process
rubrics_metrics.description: A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (or 'NPRM') typically requests public comment on a proposed rule and provides notice of any public meetings where a proposed rule will be discussed. The public comments are considered by the issuing government agency, and the text of a final rule along with a discussion of the comments is published in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notice-and-comment process is outlined in the Administrative Procedure Act and gives the public a chance to participate in agency rulemaking. Agencies publishing an NPRM must provide contact information for interested parties and are required to address concerns raised in comments when publishing the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide contact information and respond to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Any agency proposing a rule in the Federal Register must provide contact information for people and organizations interested in making comments to the agencies and the agencies are required to address these concerns when it publishes its final rule on the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically: NPRMs should include clear contact points (names, addresses, docket numbers, electronic submission instructions) so the public can submit comments; agencies should explain in the final rule how they considered and resolved substantive comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication constitutes constructive notice and is judicially noticed
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of documents in the Federal Register also constitutes constructive notice, and its contents are judicially noticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: parties are treated as having notice of what is published in the Federal Register, and courts may take judicial notice of its contents in relevant proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format: organization of each daily issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Each daily issue of the printed Federal Register is organized into four categories: Presidential Documents; Rules and Regulations (including policy statements and interpretations of rules by federal agencies); Proposed Rules (including petitions to agencies from the public); and Notices (such as scheduled hearings and meetings open to the public and grant applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When locating material or drafting citations, use the appropriate category (e.g., look under Proposed Rules for NPRMs and Notices for meeting announcements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation format for Federal Register entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations from the Federal Register are [volume] FR [page number] ([date]), e.g., 71 FR 24924 (April 7, 2006).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this standard when citing Federal Register entries in legal or administrative filings, scholarship, or rulemaking materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codification into the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules promulgated by a federal agency and published in the Federal Register are ultimately reorganized by topic or subject matter and codified in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page states the CFR is updated quarterly (and elsewhere refers to annual updates); users should confirm current CFR update cadence when relying on recodification timing. Final rules appear first in the Federal Register and are later incorporated into the CFR by subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproduction and copyright status
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no copyright restrictions on the Federal Register; as a work of the U.S. government, it is in the public domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per 1 CFR 2.6: 'Any person may reproduce or republish, without restriction, any material appearing in any regular or special edition of the Federal Register.' This permits redistribution and reuse of Federal Register content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability: official and library sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of the Federal Register may be obtained from the U.S. Government Publishing Office. Most law libraries associated with an American Bar Association-accredited law school will also have a set, as will federal depository libraries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For public access and research, check GPO, law school libraries, and federal depository libraries; historical and complete runs may be available via these channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online public access and commenting via Regulations.gov and FDMS
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations.gov was established to enable easy public access to agency dockets on rulemaking projects including the published Federal Register document. The public can use Regulations.gov to access entire rulemaking dockets from participating Federal agencies and to provide on-line comments directly to those responsible for drafting the rulemakings. The Federal Docket Management System (FDMS) is the agency side of Regulations.gov.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When participating in notice-and-comment, use Regulations.gov to find dockets, submit comments, and see supporting materials. Agencies use FDMS to manage incoming comments and docket materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programmatic access: Federal Register 2.0 and API
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Register 2.0 (launched 2010) and, in 2011, a RESTful Federal Register API were made available to facilitate programmatic access to Federal Register content. The API delivers JSON and uses HATEOAS; Ruby and Python client libraries are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the official API and client libraries for automated retrieval, searches, and integration into tools; details and developer docs are on the Office of the Federal Register developers' page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial / subscription services and coverage notes
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to official sources, the contents of the Federal Register can be acquired via several commercial databases: Citation Technologies (CyberRegs), HeinOnline (image-based PDFs back to 1936), LexisNexis (searchable text since July 1, 1980), Westlaw (searchable text since Jan 1, 1981). Certain content (e.g., Sunshine Act Meeting Notices, Unified Agenda) has specific historical coverage start dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers needing historical or searchable text access may rely on these commercial providers; check each vendor's coverage notes for date cutoffs and content inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and regulatory authorities governing Federal Register publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Register system was created under the Federal Register Act (Pub. L. 74–220, 44 U.S.C. ch. 15) and publication obligations interact with the Administrative Procedure Act (1946) and other statutes and regulations (e.g., 1 CFR provisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing procedural requirements (notice contents, rulemaking steps, timetables), consult these statutory authorities and relevant CFR provisions cited on the Federal Register/Office of the Federal Register pages.
